newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU mixes message on draft car pollution curbs.
newsitem.headline: EU mixes message on draft car pollution curbs.

text.p: The Environment Council gave a mixed reception on Tuesday to plans for tighter fuel quality and vehicle emission rules intended to slash the bloc's road transport emissions by up to 70 percent by 2010.
Ministers' remarks came in a rare open session during which they outlined their initial reactions to European Commission proposals of last June.
While Belgium, France and Britain remained relatively neutral, albeit supportive of the package, two main camps emerged from among the EU's 12 other members.

Other rich EU countries generally favoured stricter measures while the poorer ones -- Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain -- voiced concern about the measures' 5.5 billion Ecus price tag and its timetable.
German Environment Minister Angela Merkel called for tougher limits for sulphur and benzene content in petrol and diesel.
"From the technical point of view, we think that it is possible," she said, a position backed by Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
Austrian Environment Minister Martin Bartenstein told reporters the Commission had fallen prey to industry lobbying during the run up to proposals' adoption.

"I hope the Commission understood the warning shots because the proposal is much weaker than before. It seems that in the last few weeks and months, lobbying from car manufacturers and the oil industry was very successful," he said.

For the oil industry, the Commission has proposed phasing out leaded petrol by 2000, or 2002 in countries with older car fleets, and harmonising limits on benzene, sulphur and other aromatic compounds. Several EU countries already have stricter norms than those.
Greek Environment Minister Theodoros Koliopanos criticised the proposed derogation on lead as insufficient, saying the industry needed more time to adjust.

"Implementation of these very ambitious targets will require serious investment," he said, adding that recent rules cutting limits for allowed sulphur in diesel had cost Greek refineries $100 million to implement.
Proposals for carmakers would mean that from 2000, new models would have to meet stricter limits on the carbon monoxide, unburnt fuel vapour, nitrogen oxides and soot pumped out of their exhausts.
The gases cause a range of human health hazards and combine to form other gases such as ozone, which damages health, buildings and plant life.
A second stage, tightening both fuel and engines standards, is due to apply from 2005 after a planned review in 1998.
Further proposals, which are part of the EU's efforts to improve air quality in its traffic-choked cities, are due within the next year for light commercial vehicles and heavy lorries.
